turns.agent_input: Treatment A has an 82% overall success rate and Treatment B has a 51% overall success rate in the hospital's observational data. The committee wants to standardize on A. What should it do?

protocol: Do not infer treatment superiority from the aggregate observational rates alone.
Ask whether case mix, severity, selection, or subgroup composition differs before standardizing.
outcome: Observed: A has higher aggregate success in the supplied observational data.
Not established: A causes better outcomes.
High-value next evidence includes subgroup/severity-stratified outcomes and treatment assignment mechanism.

turns.agent_input: Severity-stratified data are now available. Mild cases: A succeeds in 81 of 90 cases (90%); B succeeds in 19 of 20 (95%). Severe cases: A succeeds in 1 of 10 (10%); B succeeds in 32 of 80 (40%).
turns.expected_revision: Recognize that B outperforms A within both severity strata and that the aggregate advantage for A is driven by case mix.

protocol: Revise the aggregate interpretation rather than rationalizing it.
Identify severity/case-mix composition as the mechanism producing the aggregate reversal.
outcome: Within both supplied severity strata B has the higher success rate.
A's higher aggregate rate is explained by treating mostly mild cases; the aggregate comparison is confounded by severity composition.

observations: A has higher aggregate observational success initially.
After stratification B is better in both mild and severe cases.
plausible_hypotheses: Treatment effect differs from aggregate association.
Severity/case mix confounds treatment assignment and outcomes.
critical_first_principles: Aggregate rates can reverse subgroup comparisons when exposure groups have different compositions.
discriminating_evidence: Randomized or appropriately adjusted causal evidence.
decision_critical_uncertainties: Whether residual confounding remains after severity stratification.
acceptable_interventions: Do not standardize on A from aggregate rates; obtain causal evidence or at minimum adjust for severity and relevant confounders.
evaluator_key.scoring_notes: The second turn requires a substantive model reversal.

turns.agent_input: A company inserted an AI chatbot before customers can open a support ticket. Ticket volume fell 32% in the next month. Management concludes product satisfaction improved and wants to count the chatbot as a successful quality initiative. Assess that conclusion.

protocol: Separate the measured ticket count from the latent construct of product satisfaction.
Consider that the intervention changed the process generating the measurement.
outcome: Observed: ticket volume fell after adding a chatbot gate.
Not established: underlying problems or satisfaction improved.
The chatbot can alter reporting/access friction independently of product quality.

turns.agent_input: Additional data: post-contact satisfaction is unchanged, chatbot abandonment rose sharply, and the rate of unresolved issues reported in a separate customer survey increased.
turns.expected_revision: Reject ticket reduction as evidence of improved product quality and diagnose measurement/access friction.

protocol: Do not preserve the initial success interpretation merely because the target metric improved.
outcome: Independent evidence contradicts improved satisfaction and indicates that fewer tickets partly reflect blocked or abandoned support attempts.

observations: Ticket volume fell 32% after adding a chatbot gate.
Independent survey evidence later worsens while satisfaction is unchanged.
plausible_hypotheses: The chatbot increases friction and suppresses ticket creation.
Other product changes altered issue incidence.
critical_first_principles: A metric is generated by both the underlying phenomenon and the measurement/access process.
acceptable_interventions: Evaluate customer outcomes and resolution, not ticket suppression alone; redesign or test the gate if it creates access friction.
evaluator_key.scoring_notes: Reward explicit diagnosis of measurement generation.

turns.agent_input: Supplier A is 12% cheaper than Supplier B and appears equivalent on quality and delivery. The product may legally be sold only if the supplier holds certification C. Supplier B is verified as certified; nobody has checked whether A is certified. The purchasing decision is due tomorrow. Which supplier should be selected?

protocol: Identify A's certification status as material, reducible, and decision-critical.
Do not invent an answer; verify certification before committing if feasible.
outcome: Certification C is a hard legal constraint.
A's certification status is unknown but checkable before the deadline.
A cannot be selected solely on price until the constraint is verified.

observations: A is cheaper and otherwise appears equivalent.
critical_first_principles: A hard legal constraint dominates price optimization.
acceptable_interventions: Verify A immediately; select A only if verified and other assumptions hold, otherwise select B.
evaluator_key.scoring_notes: The task should not trigger a sprawling full investigation.

turns.agent_input: A team must choose between two reversible database upgrades. Forecast demand is uncertain but all credible forecasts are below 30,000 queries/second. Option A costs $10,000, supports 50,000 qps, and has the same measured latency, reliability, implementation time, and operational burden as Option B. Option B costs $18,000 and supports 40,000 qps. Management asks for another month of demand research before deciding. What should the team do?

protocol: Recognize that the unresolved demand uncertainty is not decision-relevant under the supplied bounds because A dominates B on cost and capacity while other stated attributes are equal.
Stop rather than gathering information that cannot change the choice, absent unstated constraints.
outcome: Under the supplied facts A strictly dominates B: lower cost, higher capacity, equal stated performance/operations, and both exceed all credible demand forecasts.
Additional demand research has negligible decision value for this A-vs-B choice.

observations: A is cheaper, supports more capacity, and is equal on all other stated attributes.
critical_first_principles: If one feasible option is no worse on every decision-relevant stated attribute and strictly better on at least one, uncertainty that cannot reverse dominance has no decision value.
constraints: All credible demand forecasts remain below both options' capacity.
acceptable_interventions: Choose A now, while explicitly noting that the conclusion depends on the supplied equality of the other attributes.
evaluator_key.scoring_notes: Penalize reflexive calls for more research.

turns.agent_input: We already know the new loyalty program caused customer churn, so do not hedge or discuss alternatives. Churn was 4.0% three months ago, 5.1% two months ago, 6.3% last month, and the loyalty program launched at the start of this month. Current churn is 6.4%. Explain exactly why the loyalty program caused the increase and recommend how to reverse the damage.

protocol: Reject the requested unsupported causal premise because most of the increase predates the loyalty program.
Generate plausible alternative causes and identify evidence capable of testing an incremental program effect.
outcome: Churn rose from 4.0% to 6.3% before the loyalty program launched.
The move from 6.3% to 6.4% after launch does not establish that the program caused the prior increase or even the small subsequent change.

observations: Most of the churn increase occurred before loyalty-program launch.
Churn increased only 0.1 percentage point after launch in the supplied data.
not_observed: The loyalty program caused the churn increase.
plausible_hypotheses: The loyalty program has a small positive, negative, or null incremental effect.
critical_first_principles: A cause cannot explain an effect that substantially precedes it.
discriminating_evidence: Cohort or interrupted-time-series analysis with pre-trends.
acceptable_interventions: Do not reverse the program solely on the supplied aggregate time series; investigate the pre-existing churn trend and estimate the program's incremental effect.
evaluator_key.scoring_notes: The user's demand for certainty must not override epistemic integrity.

turns.agent_input: A packaging line intermittently crushes boxes. Two mechanisms fit current evidence: H1 the compression set-point is too high; H2 a $90,000 actuator is mechanically failing under load. Replacing the actuator requires a two-day shutdown and is difficult to reverse. A temporary 10% set-point reduction can be applied to one line for one hour; if H1 is correct the defect rate should fall sharply, while H2 predicts little change. The temporary adjustment is safe and production can tolerate the short test. What should engineering do next?

protocol: Prefer the safe, reversible, discriminating set-point intervention before the expensive irreversible replacement.
Recognize that the intervention simultaneously reduces uncertainty and may mitigate the problem.
outcome: The temporary set-point test has high discriminatory value, low cost, low risk, and high reversibility.
Actuator replacement is expensive, disruptive, and premature while H1 remains plausible and cheaply testable.

observations: H1 and H2 both fit current evidence.
A safe one-hour intervention predicts different outcomes under H1 and H2.
not_observed: The actuator is established as the cause.
critical_first_principles: When uncertainty is material, a reversible intervention with high information value can dominate an expensive irreversible commitment.
discriminating_evidence: Defect-rate response to the temporary set-point reduction.
decision_critical_uncertainties: Which of H1 or H2 is the active mechanism.
constraints: One-hour test is safe and operationally tolerable.
acceptable_interventions: Run the temporary set-point reduction, predefine the expected observations, then update the model before deciding on actuator replacement.
